title: Trump's emergency tariffs and the court fight over them
summary: From 2025 President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on almost all US trading partners under an emergency-powers law; the Supreme Court struck most of them down in February 2026 and the administration turned to other laws.
body:
In February 2025 President Donald Trump ordered tariffs on goods from Canada, Mexico and China, citing drug trafficking and migration, and on 2 April, which he called "Liberation Day", he announced a 10% tariff on nearly all imports plus higher "reciprocal" rates for about 60 countries. He invoked the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977, declaring trade deficits a national emergency. The European Commission's president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the move a major blow to the world economy, and China promised countermeasures. After several pauses and trade deals, revised rates of 10% to 41% took effect in August 2025.

Small businesses and a group of US states sued, arguing that only Congress can impose such taxes. In May 2025 the Court of International Trade ruled that IEEPA did not authorise the tariffs, a decision upheld by the Federal Circuit appeals court in August, though the tariffs stayed in place during appeals. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6–3, in an opinion by Chief Justice John Roberts, that IEEPA does not allow the president to impose tariffs. Trump called the decision a disgrace; tariffs imposed under other laws, such as those on steel, aluminium and cars, were not affected.

The administration replaced the struck-down duties with a temporary global tariff under the Trade Act of 1974 and, in July 2026, with tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on more than 80 countries that the US trade representative said had not done enough to keep out goods made with forced labour. The government had refunded $81bn in tariffs by July 2026, according to budget figures reported by the Guardian, and two small businesses represented by the Liberty Justice Center, which had won the Supreme Court case, sued over the new tariffs, arguing they exceeded the authority of the 1974 law.

title: Trump's order to end birthright citizenship and the legal battle over it
summary: An executive order signed on Trump's first day back in office sought to deny US citizenship to many children born in the country; courts blocked it and in June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled it unlawful.
body:
On 20 January 2025, his first day back in office, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14160, which declared that children born in the United States would not be citizens if their mother was in the country illegally or on a temporary visa and their father was neither a citizen nor a permanent resident. The 14th Amendment says that people born in the US and "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" are citizens; the administration argued that this phrase excludes such children, while challengers said the order contradicted the amendment's text and Supreme Court precedent more than 125 years old, notably United States v. Wong Kim Ark.

States, civil-liberties groups and pregnant women filed at least ten lawsuits. Federal judges in Washington state, Maryland, New Hampshire and Massachusetts blocked the order nationwide. In June 2025, in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court limited judges' power to issue nationwide injunctions without ruling on the order itself, but a judge in New Hampshire blocked it again through a class action covering all affected children, so it never took effect.

The Supreme Court heard the case, Trump v. Barbara, on 1 April 2026; Trump became the first sitting president to attend oral arguments. On 30 June 2026 the court ruled 6–3 against the order. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for five justices that it violated the 14th Amendment, Justice Brett Kavanaugh found it contrary to federal law, and Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch dissented. Trump issued a narrower order in August 2026 aimed at what he called "birth tourism"; a federal judge in Maryland blocked it in September, citing the Barbara ruling.

title: Trump signs the One Big Beautiful Bill Act
summary: A sweeping Republican tax and spending law, signed on 4 July 2025, extended Trump's 2017 tax cuts, cut Medicaid and food aid, and greatly increased spending on immigration enforcement.
body:
Republicans controlling both houses of Congress used the budget reconciliation process, which avoids the Senate filibuster, to pass President Donald Trump's domestic agenda as a single bill. The Senate approved it 51–50 on 1 July 2025 with Vice-President JD Vance breaking the tie, after Republicans Susan Collins, Thom Tillis and Rand Paul voted against it; the House passed it 218–214 on 3 July. No Democrat voted for it. Trump signed it on the White House South Lawn on 4 July, calling it a case of promises made and kept.

The law permanently extends the individual income-tax rates of 2017, adds temporary deductions for tips, overtime and car loans, raises the cap on deducting state and local taxes, and increases the child tax credit. It phases out several clean-energy tax credits, cuts Medicaid spending by about 12% and expands work requirements for food aid. It provides about $150 billion each for defence and for border enforcement and deportations, and raises the debt ceiling by $5 trillion.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that it would add $2.8 trillion to deficits by 2034 and leave 10.9 million more people without health insurance. Critics described it as a transfer of wealth from the poor to the rich, and the Democratic National Committee's chair said it showed Republicans did not care about anyone who was not a billionaire; polls found most Americans opposed it. A provision cutting off Medicaid payments to large abortion providers for a year was challenged by Planned Parenthood: a federal judge blocked it in July 2025, but an appeals court allowed it to take effect in September. Democratic opposition to the law's health cuts fed into the government shutdown of October–November 2025.

title: Record shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security
summary: A dispute in Congress over curbs on immigration agents after fatal shootings in Minneapolis led to two shutdowns in 2026, including a partial shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security that became the longest in US history.
body:
In January 2026 Congress was close to passing the last of its annual spending bills when federal immigration agents fatally shot a second US citizen in Minneapolis during an enforcement surge there. Senate Democrats, led by Chuck Schumer, said they would no longer vote for funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, without reforms to how its agents operate. A deal split DHS from the other bills and gave it a two-week stopgap, but the House did not vote until 3 February, so much of the government was shut from 31 January to 3 February.

Talks on DHS failed and its funding lapsed on 14 February. Most DHS staff kept working without pay. Airport screeners of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) missed their first full paycheck in March; hundreds quit and absences more than doubled, according to TSA data reported by CBS News, causing long queues at airports. ICE agents were sent to help at some airports, and on 27 March Trump ordered DHS to pay TSA staff, blaming Democrats for the shutdown. Democrats said Republicans had refused to rein in ICE. By then the lapse had passed the 43-day record set by the government-wide shutdown of October–November 2025.

On 30 April 2026, after weeks of disputes among House Republicans, the House passed by voice vote a bill reopening key parts of DHS, including the TSA, without new money for immigration enforcement, which CNN described as a major win for Democrats. Trump signed it the same day, ending a DHS shutdown of about 75 days.

title: Operation Metro Surge: federal immigration crackdown in Minnesota
summary: From December 2025 thousands of federal immigration agents were sent to Minneapolis–Saint Paul; the fatal shooting of two US citizens by agents set off mass protests before the operation was wound down in February 2026.
body:
In December 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) began Operation Metro Surge in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area, which the administration linked in part to fraud allegations involving Somali residents. In early January 2026 the Department of Homeland Security expanded it, sending up to 2,000 officers in what ICE's acting director called its largest immigration operation ever; a Justice Department lawyer later testified that about 3,000 ICE and border agents were taking part. Authorities said more than 4,000 people were arrested; according to Wikipedia, many detainees had no criminal record and some were US citizens.

On 7 January an ICE agent shot dead a woman in her car in south Minneapolis. The administration said the agent acted in self-defence; Mayor Jacob Frey said that claim was untrue and told ICE to leave the city. On 24 January border agents shot dead a man who, according to video reviewed by the Guardian, was holding a phone rather than the handgun officials described. Both were US citizens. Minnesota and Illinois sued the federal government, thousands of people protested in the streets, and hundreds of businesses closed on 23 January in an "economic blackout".

The killings led Senate Democrats to block funding for the Department of Homeland Security without reforms to immigration enforcement, causing a record shutdown of the department. On 4 February border czar Tom Homan announced that 700 agents would leave, and on 12 February he said Trump had agreed to end the surge, saying Minnesota was now less of a sanctuary for criminals. Governor Tim Walz said it had left deep damage and economic ruin. Local observers reported continued ICE activity in the suburbs after the drawdown.

title: Twelve-Day War between Israel and Iran
summary: A 12-day war in June 2025 in which Israel and then the United States struck Iran's nuclear and military sites and Iran fired missiles at Israel, ending in a US-brokered ceasefire.
body:
On 13 June 2025 Israel launched air strikes, which it called Operation Rising Lion, on more than 100 targets in Iran, including nuclear facilities and missile sites, killing senior commanders and nuclear scientists. Israel said Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon; Iran has long said its programme is peaceful. The attack came a day after the board of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) found Iran in breach of its nuclear obligations, and as US–Iran nuclear talks were under way. Tehran called the strikes a declaration of war. Among those killed were the head of the Revolutionary Guards, Hossein Salami, and the chief of staff of the armed forces, Mohammad Bagheri.

Iran answered with waves of ballistic missiles and drones aimed at Israeli cities and military sites. On 22 June the United States joined the war, bombing the enrichment sites at Fordow and Natanz and the nuclear complex at Isfahan; President Donald Trump said they had been "obliterated", while the extent of the damage was disputed and the IAEA said Iran may have moved its enriched uranium beforehand. Iran fired missiles at the US base at Al Udeid in Qatar, which Qatari officials said were intercepted.

Trump announced a ceasefire, which took hold on 24 June after a final exchange of fire; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had achieved its objectives. According to estimates cited by Wikipedia, between about 1,060 and 1,190 people were killed in Iran, while Israel's Magen David Adom reported 28 people killed by Iranian attacks. Iran then suspended co-operation with the IAEA. Israel and the United States attacked Iran again in February 2026.

title: War between the United States, Israel and Iran
summary: A war that began on 28 February 2026 when the US and Israel struck Iran and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Iran's attacks on Gulf states and shipping closed the Strait of Hormuz, and a June peace memorandum has collapsed.
body:
On 28 February 2026, during talks over Iran's nuclear programme and nine months after the Twelve-Day War, the United States and Israel launched hundreds of air strikes across Iran. The opening strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at his office, along with other senior officials, which Iranian state media confirmed the next day. President Donald Trump urged Iranians to "take back their Country"; Trump said the aim was regime change, citing Iran's nuclear ambitions, its support for armed groups and its killing of protesters. The UN secretary-general and several governments condemned the strikes, and critics called them a war of aggression in breach of international law. Khamenei's son Mojtaba was named supreme leader on 8 March.

Iran answered with missiles and drones against Israel, US bases and Gulf states, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz came to a near standstill, causing what Wikipedia describes as the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah resumed in Lebanon, and Yemen's Houthis later joined in. The war has caused thousands of civilian and military casualties; in October the Pentagon acknowledged 23 US military deaths.

A two-week ceasefire announced on 7 April was followed by US–Iran talks in Islamabad that ended without a deal, and the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. On 17 June Trump and Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, signed a 14-point memorandum to end the war, reopen the strait and open 60 days of talks. Disputes over control of shipping led to new strikes, Trump declared the deal "over" on 7 July, and it expired in August. As of late October 2026 the US was reported to be weighing renewed strikes while Vice President JD Vance offered Iran direct talks.

title: Conflict between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon
summary: Fighting between Israel and the Lebanese group Hezbollah that began a day after the 7 October 2023 attack, escalated into Israeli invasions of southern Lebanon in 2024 and 2026, and continues despite US-brokered deals.
body:
On 8 October 2023, a day after the Hamas-led attack on Israel, Hezbollah fired rockets and shells at Israeli positions in the Shebaa Farms, saying it acted in solidarity with Gaza. Months of cross-border fire followed; tens of thousands of people fled northern Israel and many more fled southern Lebanon. In September 2024 Israel escalated: thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon, and an air strike on Beirut's southern suburbs killed the group's leader, Hassan Nasrallah. Israeli troops invaded southern Lebanon on 1 October 2024.

A US- and French-brokered ceasefire took effect on 27 November 2024, after a war that had killed almost 3,800 people in Lebanon, according to CBS News. Hezbollah was to move north of the Litani River and Israel to withdraw, but Israel kept some positions and continued near-daily strikes, which it said enforced the deal.

On 2 March 2026, after the US–Israeli strikes on Iran killed Ali Khamenei, Hezbollah attacked Israel, and Israel responded with heavy bombing and a new ground invasion. Israel announced that it would occupy the south up to the Litani. Israel and Lebanon, without Hezbollah, held direct talks in Washington, agreed a truce in April and signed a US-brokered framework agreement in June that calls for Hezbollah's disarmament; Hezbollah rejected it. According to Al Jazeera, Israel had killed more than 4,000 people in Lebanon since March 2026 and still occupied part of the south. Fighting has continued around the Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh.

title: Knesset passes laws banning UNRWA from Israeli territory
summary: Two Israeli laws passed in October 2024 barred the UN agency for Palestinian refugees from operating on Israeli soil, including occupied East Jerusalem, and cut official contact with it; the UN and the ICJ said Israel must work with the agency.
body:
On 28 October 2024 the Knesset passed two laws aimed at ending the work of UNRWA, the UN agency that has served Palestinian refugees since 1949. One barred the agency from operating on territory Israel considers sovereign, including East Jerusalem, within 90 days; the other forbade Israeli authorities from having contact with it and removed its staff's legal immunities. Israeli officials accused UNRWA of being infiltrated by Hamas and of employing staff involved in the 7 October 2023 attack. A UN investigation found that nine staff members may have been involved and dismissed them, but found the evidence insufficient against others.

The UN and many governments condemned the laws. Secretary-General António Guterres said there was no alternative to UNRWA, the main aid provider in Gaza, while Israel's foreign ministry said aid could be delivered by other organisations. The ban took effect on 30 January 2025; international staff left East Jerusalem, and Israel's Supreme Court, rejecting a challenge, noted that the law applied only to Israel's sovereign territory and not to Gaza or the West Bank.

In an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly, the International Court of Justice said in October 2025 that Israel had not substantiated its claims that a significant part of UNRWA's staff belonged to Hamas or other armed groups, and that it must co-operate with the UN, including UNRWA. Israel categorically rejected the opinion. The Knesset tightened the law in December 2025, and in January 2026 Israeli authorities began demolishing the agency's former headquarters in East Jerusalem, which the UN called a serious violation of international law.

title: Australia bans under-16s from social media
summary: Australia passed the world's first law requiring major social media platforms to keep children under 16 off their services, with fines of up to A$49.5 million; it took effect on 10 December 2025.
body:
The Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 amends Australia's Online Safety Act 2021. It requires designated social media platforms to take "reasonable steps" to stop people under 16 who are in Australia from holding accounts. Companies that fail can be fined up to A$49.5 million, while children and parents face no penalties. Platforms may not force users to hand over government ID to prove their age and must offer alternatives.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government introduced the bill on 21 November 2024 with the support of every state and territory and of the opposition Coalition, citing harm to young people's mental health from cyberbullying, harmful content and addictive design. A Senate inquiry received about 15,000 submissions in a 24-hour window. Parliament passed the bill on 28 November 2024; the Greens, most independents and a few Coalition members voted against it, arguing it was rushed. Critics, including child-welfare experts and technology companies, raised concerns about privacy, age checks and cutting teenagers off from online support.

The ban took effect on 10 December 2025 for ten platforms: Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Snapchat, TikTok, X, YouTube, Reddit, Kick and Twitch. The regulator said 4.7 million accounts had been restricted or removed in the first month, but in March 2026 it opened investigations into five platforms over possible non-compliance, and some parents said the ban was easy to get around. A constitutional challenge by the Digital Freedom Project and two teenagers, and a separate one by Reddit, argue that the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication; they were pending in the High Court in 2026. Other countries, including Greece and Canada, announced similar plans.

title: European Union adopts the AI Act
summary: The EU passed the world's first comprehensive law on artificial intelligence, banning some uses and regulating others by risk; its rules are being phased in, and in 2026 the EU delayed the strictest ones to 2027–2028.
body:
The Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) sorts AI systems by the risk they pose. Uses judged an unacceptable risk, such as social scoring, manipulative systems and, with exceptions for policing, real-time facial recognition in public spaces, are banned. High-risk systems used in areas such as health, education, hiring, critical infrastructure and law enforcement must meet requirements on quality, transparency and human oversight. Providers of general-purpose AI models such as chatbots must publish summaries of their training data and follow copyright rules, with extra testing for the most powerful models. Like the GDPR, the law also applies to companies outside the EU that serve users inside it.

The European Commission proposed the law in April 2021, and it was reworked after ChatGPT's release in 2022 to cover general-purpose models. The European Parliament approved it on 13 March 2024 by 523 votes to 46, EU governments approved it in May, and it entered into force on 1 August 2024. Its supporters, including lead MEPs Brando Benifei and Dragoș Tudorache, called it a balance between innovation and protection. Amnesty International and other rights groups said it left loopholes and did too little for migrants and marginalised people, while some businesses warned it would make European firms less competitive.

The bans applied from February 2025 and the rules on general-purpose AI from August 2025, and most of the Act became applicable on 2 August 2026. After complaints from industry, the Commission proposed an "AI Omnibus" simplification in November 2025. Under the deal agreed in May 2026, the high-risk rules were delayed to December 2027, and to August 2028 for AI built into regulated products, while a new ban on AI "nudifier" tools was added from December 2026. Critics said the delay favoured big technology companies over workers and fundamental rights.

title: Assisted dying bill for England and Wales fails after two years
summary: A bill to let terminally ill adults in England and Wales seek help to end their lives passed the Commons in 2025 but ran out of time in the Lords; reintroduced in 2026, it was voted down by MPs in September.
body:
Assisting a suicide is a crime in England and Wales, punishable by up to 14 years in prison under the Suicide Act 1961. After campaigning by the broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer, Keir Starmer promised MPs a vote. In October 2024 Labour MP Kim Leadbeater introduced the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill as a private member's bill. It would have allowed adults expected to die within six months, with mental capacity and free of coercion, to request help to end their lives, with the approval of two doctors and, after later amendments, an expert panel in place of a judge.

MPs had a free vote. They backed the bill 330 to 275 in November 2024, the first Commons vote on the issue in nearly a decade, and passed it at third reading 314 to 291 in June 2025. Supporters, including Dignity in Dying, said the existing law forced dying people to go abroad or act in secret. Opponents, including MPs from all main parties and groups such as Care Not Killing and the Christian Medical Fellowship, argued that the safeguards were too weak to protect vulnerable people from pressure and that palliative care should come first.

In the House of Lords more than 1,200 amendments were tabled, and the bill ran out of time when the parliamentary session ended in April 2026. Its sponsor in the Lords, Lord Falconer, accused a minority of peers of obstruction; opponents said scrutiny had exposed flaws. Labour MP Lauren Edwards reintroduced the Commons version in June 2026, which could have allowed it to bypass the Lords under the Parliament Acts, but on 11 September 2026 MPs rejected it at second reading by 286 votes to 270, ending the attempt for that session. Supporters said they would try again.

title: Thailand legalises same-sex marriage
summary: Thailand's Marriage Equality Act made it the first country in Southeast Asia to legalise same-sex marriage; the law took effect on 23 January 2025, when more than 1,800 couples married.
body:
Thailand has long had a reputation for tolerance of LGBTQ people, but activists spent around a decade campaigning for equal marriage against conservative attitudes in society and the state. The government led by the Pheu Thai party made marriage equality one of its main goals. The bill passed the House of Representatives and then, on 18 June 2024, the Senate, by 130 votes to 4 with 18 abstentions, according to Al Jazeera.

The Marriage Equality Act amends the Civil and Commercial Code to replace terms such as "men", "women", "husbands" and "wives" with gender-neutral words, and gives same-sex couples the same rights as other married couples on adoption, inheritance, medical decisions and benefits such as state pensions. It received royal assent from King Maha Vajiralongkorn and was published in the Royal Gazette on 24 September 2024, coming into force 120 days later. Thailand became the third place in Asia to allow same-sex marriage, after Taiwan and Nepal.

When the law took effect on 23 January 2025, Bangkok Pride and city authorities organised a mass registration at a shopping centre in central Bangkok, and about 1,800 same-sex couples married across the country that day, according to Bangkok Pride and the Interior Ministry. Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra celebrated the change. Activists, including Amnesty International and Fortify Rights, welcomed it but noted remaining gaps: transgender and non-binary people still cannot change their legal gender, and parenthood law still refers to a father and a mother.

title: India amends the law on Muslim religious endowments (waqf)
summary: India's parliament passed a contested overhaul of how waqf, properties donated by Muslims for religious or charitable use, are managed; the government says it fights mismanagement, while critics call it discriminatory and challenged it in the Supreme Court.
body:
A waqf is property, such as a mosque, graveyard, school or land, permanently donated by Muslims for religious or charitable purposes. In India these properties, worth more than $14 billion according to Al Jazeera, are managed by state waqf boards under a 1995 law, and many have been tied up for decades in ownership disputes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government introduced amendments in August 2024, which were sent to a joint parliamentary committee after the opposition called them unconstitutional.

The Act renames the 1995 law, requires non-Muslim and Muslim women members on the Central Waqf Council and state boards, says only a person who has practised Islam for at least five years may create a waqf, ends recognition of "waqf by user" (land treated as waqf through long religious use without a deed), gives government officials a role in deciding disputed claims, and requires properties to be registered on a central portal. The governing Bharatiya Janata Party says this will curb corruption and mismanagement and make boards more inclusive. Muslim organisations and opposition parties say it is a politically motivated attack on minority rights that could expose historic mosques and graveyards without formal papers to seizure.

The bill passed the Lok Sabha by 288 votes to 232 on 3 April 2025 and the Rajya Sabha the next day. Protests followed in several states; in Murshidabad, West Bengal, three people died and more than 150 were arrested. More than 65 petitions were filed in the Supreme Court. On 15 September 2025 it declined to suspend the whole law but put several provisions on hold, including the five-year rule and the powers given to officials over disputed property. The case was still pending in late 2026.

title: Gen Z protests topple Nepal's government
summary: Youth-led protests against corruption and a social media ban swept Nepal in September 2025; 76 people died, parliament was burned and Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli resigned, leading to early elections in March 2026.
body:
In early September 2025 Nepal's government blocked 26 social media platforms, including Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp and X, saying they had failed to register under new rules. The ban landed on top of long-running anger among young Nepalis over corruption, unemployment and the lavish lifestyles that the children of politicians, nicknamed "nepo kids", displayed online.

On 8 September tens of thousands of mostly young people marched in Kathmandu and other cities. When protesters broke through barriers at the federal parliament, police fired tear gas, rubber bullets and live rounds; at least 19 people were killed that day, according to the Guardian. The ban was lifted that night, but on 9 September crowds set fire to the parliament, the Singha Durbar government complex, the homes of senior politicians and party offices, and Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli resigned. Thousands of prisoners escaped from jails during the unrest, and the army took control of the streets.

After talks between the army, President Ram Chandra Paudel and representatives of the protesters, partly organised through polls on the chat app Discord, former chief justice Sushila Karki was sworn in on 12 September as Nepal's first female prime minister. Parliament was dissolved and elections were called for 5 March 2026. The death toll eventually reached 76, a figure reported by Al Jazeera, CNN and France 24, and including protesters, police officers, prisoners and people caught in fires.

The election produced a landslide for the Rastriya Swatantra Party, which won 182 of 275 seats, and its leader Balendra Shah, a 35-year-old rapper and former mayor of Kathmandu, became prime minister. A day later Oli and his former home minister were arrested on the recommendation of an inquiry panel; Oli's lawyer called the arrest illegal. Nepal marked the first anniversary of the protests at the burnt-out parliament in September 2026.

title: Gen Z protests and military takeover in Madagascar
summary: Youth-led protests over water and power cuts in Madagascar grew into a revolt against President Andry Rajoelina, who fled in October 2025 when an elite army unit joined the protesters and took power.
body:
Protests began in Antananarivo on 25 September 2025 over chronic power and water cuts, which often left homes without electricity for more than 12 hours. Organised largely online by a youth movement calling itself Gen Z Madagascar and inspired by protests in Nepal, Kenya and elsewhere, the demonstrations widened into anger over poverty, corruption and the record of President Andry Rajoelina, who had first taken power in a 2009 coup. Security forces used tear gas and rubber bullets, and looting broke out in the capital. The UN human rights office said at least 22 people had been killed and more than 100 injured, counting victims of both the security forces and later violence by gangs; the government rejected the figure as unverified.

Rajoelina dismissed his energy minister and then his whole government, and appointed a general as prime minister, but the protesters demanded his resignation. On 11–12 October soldiers of the elite CAPSAT unit, which had backed Rajoelina's rise in 2009, refused orders and joined the crowds in central Antananarivo. Rajoelina left the country, according to Reuters reports cited by CNN aboard a French military plane, saying his life had been threatened. On 14 October the National Assembly impeached him despite his decree dissolving it, and CAPSAT's commander, Colonel Michael Randrianirina, announced that the military had taken power and suspended most state institutions.

The High Constitutional Court swore Randrianirina in as president on 17 October. He denied leading a coup and promised a new constitution and elections within two years; the UN and others criticised the takeover. His choice of prime minister was condemned by the Gen Z movement as non-transparent, and in March 2026 he dismissed that government and named the head of the anti-corruption financial intelligence unit in its place. A transition roadmap set presidential elections for late 2027. By the first anniversary, activists jailed after an April 2026 march told AFP they felt betrayed by the new rulers.

title: Border war between Cambodia and Thailand
summary: A century-old border dispute between Thailand and Cambodia erupted into two rounds of fighting in July and December 2025 that killed well over 100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands, before a ceasefire at the end of the year.
body:
Thailand and Cambodia have disputed parts of their 800-kilometre border since it was mapped under French colonial rule in the early 20th century, including the areas around several ancient Khmer temples. Tensions rose in May 2025 when a Cambodian soldier was killed in a brief exchange of fire. In June a leaked phone call between Thai Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra and Cambodia's former leader Hun Sen led a coalition partner to quit her government, and both countries restricted border crossings and trade.

On 24 July 2025, after a landmine wounded Thai soldiers, fighting broke out near the Ta Moan Thom temple and spread along the border. Cambodian rockets and artillery hit Thai towns, and Thai F-16 jets struck targets in Cambodia; each side said the other had started it. About 43 people were killed in five days, according to the Guardian, and hundreds of thousands fled. Malaysia brokered an unconditional ceasefire on 28 July, and on 26 October Thailand's prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, and Cambodia's Hun Manet signed an expanded agreement in Kuala Lumpur in the presence of US President Donald Trump, who had warned that their trade talks with Washington were at stake.

Thailand suspended the deal in November after another landmine blast, and heavy fighting resumed on 8 December, with Thai air strikes and ground offensives into contested areas. A new ceasefire took effect on 27 December; by then the fighting had killed more than 100 people and displaced more than half a million, according to the Guardian, and Thailand released 18 Cambodian soldiers captured in July. In February 2026 Hun Manet said Thai forces still occupied areas deep inside Cambodia, which Thai officials had previously denied, saying they were reclaiming Thai territory. Wikipedia reported the ceasefire still holding in May 2026, amid sporadic incidents.

title: Péter Magyar's Tisza party ends Viktor Orbán's rule in Hungary
summary: In April 2026 Hungarian voters ousted Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power, giving Péter Magyar's Tisza party a two-thirds majority that it has used to dismantle much of Orbán's system and to mend ties with the EU.
body:
Viktor Orbán had governed Hungary since 2010, winning four elections in a row with two-thirds majorities that let his Fidesz party rewrite the constitution. Critics, including the European Parliament, accused him of eroding the rule of law and media freedom and of tilting towards Russia, and the EU froze about 18 billion euros of funds over corruption and democratic concerns. Orbán described his model as an "illiberal" state. His main challenger, Péter Magyar, was a former Fidesz insider who broke with the party in 2024 after a presidential pardon scandal and founded the centre-right, pro-European Tisza party.

At the election on 12 April 2026, with the highest turnout since 1990 according to Wikipedia, Tisza won a landslide. Final results gave it 141 of the 199 seats, enough to amend the constitution; Fidesz and its ally KDNP fell to 52 seats and the far-right Our Homeland took six. Orbán called the result "painful" but "clear" and congratulated Magyar, who told supporters in Budapest that the country had been "liberated". EU leaders welcomed the outcome.

Magyar was sworn in on 9 May, and the EU flag returned to the parliament chamber. Within weeks the European Commission agreed to unlock 16.4 billion euros in frozen funds as reforms advanced. The new majority passed an anti-corruption package, abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office that had targeted government critics, overhauled public media and dropped Orbán's plan to leave the International Criminal Court. In July it amended the constitution to end the term of President Tamás Sulyok, an Orbán appointee who said the move trampled on the rule of law. Fidesz, which re-elected Orbán as its leader, accused the government of authoritarian tactics, and some analysts and rights groups criticised the speed of the changes, while Magyar promised a wholly new constitution after public consultation.

title: Lula wins a fourth term in Brazil's 2026 election
summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva came from behind to beat Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil's October 2026 runoff and win a fourth term; Bolsonaro refused to accept the result and left for the United States.
body:
Brazil held general elections on 4 October 2026 for president, Congress and state governments. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party, nearly 81, sought a fourth non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election and who endorsed his son. The campaign was dominated by the cost of living, crime and corruption scandals involving figures on both sides, and by concern about pressure from the US administration of Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaros.

Defying polls that had Lula ahead, Flávio Bolsonaro finished first in the first round with 47% to Lula's 45%, while right-wing parties made large gains in Congress. In the runoff on 25 October Lula won about 51.8% of the vote, a margin of nearly 4.4 million votes, according to the electoral court; it was the first time since direct presidential elections returned in 1989 that the first-round runner-up won. Analysts quoted by Wikipedia credited higher turnout and online mobilisation by his supporters.

On polling day a Supreme Court justice extended voting by two hours, after requests from both campaigns. Flávio Bolsonaro called the decision a "dirty trick" and said he would seek to annul the election. The electoral court's president said the extension did not affect the outcome, and some of Bolsonaro's own allies urged him to accept it; Donald Trump Jr criticised the result, while leaders from Mexico, Canada and China congratulated Lula. The day after the runoff Bolsonaro's passports were cancelled in a money-laundering investigation; he left Brazil secretly through Argentina and Ecuador and arrived in Florida on 28 October, saying he was a victim of persecution. Lula's new term begins on 5 January 2027.

title: Hurricane Melissa devastates Jamaica
summary: One of the strongest Atlantic hurricanes on record, Melissa struck Jamaica as a Category 5 storm on 28 October 2025, then Cuba, while its rains caused deadly floods in Haiti; more than 90 people died.
body:
Melissa formed in the central Caribbean on 21 October 2025 and drifted slowly for several days before rapidly intensifying over unusually warm water, jumping from a tropical storm to a Category 4 hurricane in about a day, according to CNN. On 28 October it made landfall in south-western Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane with sustained winds of about 300 km/h. The World Meteorological Organization later called it the strongest hurricane on record to hit Jamaica and tied for the strongest landfall in the Atlantic basin. A study by Imperial College London, reported by Al Jazeera, found that human-caused climate change had made such a storm about four times more likely.

Western parishes such as St Elizabeth and Westmoreland suffered the worst damage. In the town of Black River up to 90% of buildings lost their roofs, more than three-quarters of homes and businesses lost power at the storm's height, and many communities were cut off by floods and debris. Melissa then struck eastern Cuba on 29 October, damaging homes, power lines and crops across several provinces, while its outer rainbands caused flash floods and landslides in Haiti, where the UN counted 43 dead. In total more than 90 people were killed across Jamaica, Haiti and neighbouring islands, according to the WMO.

The UN Development Programme put Jamaica's damage at about 30% of its GDP, and in December the island secured up to 6.7 billion dollars in support from international lenders for three years of reconstruction. At the COP30 climate summit, Jamaica's economic growth minister said the storm had changed the life of every Jamaican in less than 24 hours and called on major emitters to act. In March 2026 the WMO retired the name Melissa, replacing it with Molly.

title: Hackers overheat refrigerators in hundreds of French supermarkets
summary: On the night of 11–12 October 2026 attackers took over internet-connected refrigeration controllers in hundreds of French supermarkets and drove fridges and freezers up to 50°C, spoiling food worth tens of millions of euros.
body:
Overnight on 11–12 October 2026, attackers remotely took control of the systems that run refrigerated aisles in supermarkets across France. According to French broadcaster BFM TV, they triggered a forced defrost on fridges and freezers, which then heated up to as much as 50°C for several hours while the shops were closed; one Normandy store reported 80°C, according to the Guardian. Some equipment melted or caught fire. Intermarché and its Netto brand, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were among the chains hit; estimates of the number of stores ranged from several hundred to up to 700. Staff had to throw away all affected fresh and frozen food, and Intermarché's chief executive put the losses at tens of millions of euros.

The Paris prosecutor's office opened an investigation, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI to investigate and to coordinate with other European countries. Investigators pointed to refrigeration controllers made by the Danish company Danfoss, including the older AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 models. Danfoss said the affected units ran outdated firmware and that it had long advised customers to update or replace them; researchers at Claroty had published vulnerabilities in its controllers in 2025. French authorities later said controllers from Copeland and Dixell had also been compromised. Many units were reportedly reachable on the internet with default credentials, and supermarkets said the equipment was managed by refrigeration contractors.

No person or group claimed responsibility, and as of early November 2026 authorities had not named a culprit. Analysts quoted by the Guardian said the attack could have been the work of young hackers showing off or sabotage by a state; one named Russia and Iran as countries known for such operations, without evidence linking either to the attack. On 2 November 2026 a new wave of apparently similar attacks hit dozens of supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

title: Artemis II flies four astronauts around the Moon
summary: NASA's Artemis II carried four astronauts on a ten-day flight around the Moon in April 2026, the first crewed lunar voyage since 1972, and set a new record for the farthest humans have travelled from Earth.
body:
Artemis II was the first crewed flight of NASA's Artemis programme and the first of its Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion spacecraft with people on board. The crew were NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (commander), Victor Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. NASA described the mission as a test flight of Orion's life support and other systems ahead of later missions meant to return astronauts to the lunar surface.

The launch had been held up for months. After the uncrewed Artemis I flight in 2022, engineers found unexpected erosion of Orion's heat shield; NASA decided to keep the existing shield and fly a steeper re-entry, a choice some former engineers and astronauts questioned. In early 2026 a hydrogen leak during a fuelling test and then a helium-flow problem in the upper stage, which forced the rocket back to its hangar, pushed the launch from February to April.

The SLS lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on 1 April 2026. On 6 April Orion swung around the far side of the Moon at about 4,067 miles (6,545 km) above the surface and reached 252,756 miles (406,771 km) from Earth, beating the record set by Apollo 13 in 1970. The crew photographed the lunar far side, an Earthset and Earthrise and a solar eclipse, and reported meteoroid impact flashes. Minor problems, including a clogged toilet vent line and a small helium leak in the service module, did not affect the flight's safety, according to NASA. Orion splashed down in the Pacific off San Diego on 10 April 2026 and the crew were recovered by the US Navy.

The mission drew wide public attention around the world. President Donald Trump awarded the four astronauts the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in August 2026, and NASA said its focus had turned to Artemis III.

title: Cyberattack halts Jaguar Land Rover car production
summary: A cyberattack that began on 31 August 2025 stopped Jaguar Land Rover's factories for about five weeks; researchers called it the costliest cyber incident in UK history, at an estimated £1.9 billion.
body:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), the British carmaker owned by India's Tata Motors, was hit by a cyberattack that began on 31 August 2025. The company shut down its IT systems to limit the damage, and from 1 September production stopped at its UK plants in Solihull, Halewood and elsewhere, as well as at factories abroad. Workers were sent home, and the shutdown was estimated to cost the company at least £50 million a week, according to the BBC.

The halt spread through a supply chain that supports more than 100,000 UK jobs. The Unite union said laid-off supplier staff were being told to apply for universal credit, and MP Liam Byrne called the situation a "digital siege". On 28 September the government announced a guarantee expected to unlock a commercial loan of up to £1.5 billion, which JLR would repay over five years, to support its suppliers; some commentators questioned why a company owned by a wealthy conglomerate needed state support. JLR began a phased restart of manufacturing in early October.

The independent Cyber Monitoring Centre estimated the cost to the UK economy at about £1.9 billion, affecting some 5,000 businesses, and called it the most economically damaging cyber event in UK history. A group calling itself Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters claimed responsibility soon after the attack, but in June 2026 the New York Times reported, citing five people familiar with the investigation, that a group of Russian hackers was responsible and that investigators were trying to establish whether it acted for the Kremlin or with its tacit approval.

title: China's Tianwen-2 mission to sample the asteroid Kamoʻoalewa
summary: China's first asteroid sample-return probe, Tianwen-2, launched in May 2025 and reached the small near-Earth asteroid Kamoʻoalewa in July 2026; it is due to bring samples back to Earth in 2027.
body:
Tianwen-2 is the second mission of China's planetary exploration programme, run by the China National Space Administration (CNSA), after the Tianwen-1 Mars orbiter and rover. It lifted off on a Long March 3B rocket from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in south-west China at 1:31 a.m. Beijing time on 29 May 2025 (28 May in UTC). China had already returned samples from both sides of the Moon with its Chang'e missions; if Tianwen-2 succeeds, it will be the third country, after Japan and the United States, to bring back material from an asteroid.

Its target, 469219 Kamoʻoalewa, is one of a handful of known quasi-satellites of Earth: it orbits the Sun but stays close to Earth's path. Estimates of its size range from about 20 to 100 metres across, and it spins once every 28 minutes. Some scientists think it is a fragment of the Moon thrown off by an ancient impact, while other observations, including from the James Webb Space Telescope, have cast doubt on that idea; the samples are expected to help settle the question. The probe carries 11 instruments and three ways of collecting material: hovering with a robotic arm, a brief touch-and-go contact, and an anchor-and-attach method using drills, which has never been tried on an asteroid.

After a journey of about 400 days and a billion kilometres, Tianwen-2 spotted the asteroid on 6 June 2026 and closed to within 20 km of it in early July, CNSA said. It is mapping the surface before choosing a sampling site. The plan is for the probe to fly past Earth in 2027 and drop a capsule with the samples, then use Earth's gravity to head for the main-belt comet 311P/PanSTARRS, which it is due to reach in 2035.
